lines.text: Every order a company ships comes with a promise: a delivery date.
Aisha Rahman in Liverpool was promised hers by December 14th.
On October 20th, a cyber incident shuts the terminals at the Port of Singapore.
Her parcel never goes near Singapore. It will still be late.
Radio modules get stuck at the port. The circuit boards waiting on them slip, then the smart home devices, the warehouse restock, and her parcel.
Four steps down the chain, she's three days late.
Across the network: 755 late orders, $114,000 in fees, and nobody sees it coming.
This is Promise Graph.
It finds every broken promise, works out what to rescue, and runs AI agents that remember what worked.
Underneath is a FalkorDB graph: ports, lanes, shipments that feed each other, and orders with promises.
A closed port is a starting node. The damage is a path, and one Cypher query walks it.
Ask in plain English, and you get one sentence and a graph of only what answers it.
The AI only picks a question template. Every number comes from Cypher.
See it on the globe, or step by step: what FalkorDB walked, how long it took, and the exact query.
Ask why Aisha's order is late: the chain back to the port, then the same chain on a calendar.
Or ask for the costliest orders, what to rescue first, or a way around the port.
Then six AI agents take over, and they coordinate through the graph.
Sentinel recalls similar disruptions, the Impact Analyst traces the damage, the Rerouter finds routes, Finance prices each rescue, and the Verifier rechecks the numbers.
Each agent writes its decision as a node, and the next one reads it from there. The graph is their shared workspace and their audit trail.
In about a second, they propose rerouting three shipments by sea for $19,000, saving $68,000.
Spending needs approval, and never from the person who asked.
The Agents view draws the run as the graph they wrote. On the globe, you can watch them walk it.
Now, memory. Every approved plan records what it expected to save, and later, what it actually saved.
At Suez in July, air freight cost $96,000 and delivered only 28 percent of the saving it promised. Sea reroutes delivered 95.
In November, LA and Long Beach go on strike: $681,000 in late fees.
At face value, air-freighting five shipments for $409,000 looks like a bargain.
But Finance remembers Suez. At 28 percent, the rescue saves less than it costs, so it recommends no rescue, and shows which memory changed its mind.
Rerun without memory, and the agents would have paid for the air freight. Memory avoided an expected $220,000 loss.
Everything runs on FalkorDB. Postgres is only a baseline that returns identical rows.
On deep chains FalkorDB pulls ahead, and we documented three of its bugs along the way.
Take FalkorDB out, and nothing runs.
Promise Graph. See every broken promise, rescue what matters, and learn from what actually worked.
